## Roadmap

In this tutorial, we will:

1. Investigate **complete separation** in logistic regression and see how regularization helps.
2. Compare **logistic regression, LDA, and QDA** on the **Smarket** data.
3. Compare **multinomial logistic regression, LDA, and QDA** on the **iris** data, including their decision regions.
4. Discuss how model assumptions, flexibility, and test accuracy relate to model choice.

### Setup

Run the following installation command **only if** any of the packages are missing:

```{r install-packages, eval=FALSE}
install.packages(c("ISLR2", "MASS", "glmnet", "nnet", "ggplot2"))
```

```{r setup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(ISLR2)     # Smarket dataset
library(MASS)      # lda() and qda()
library(glmnet)    # Regularized logistic regression
library(nnet)      # Multinomial logistic regression
library(ggplot2)   # Plots

set.seed(0)
```

## 1. Warm-up: Complete separation in logistic regression

For binary logistic regression, we model

$$
P(Y=1\mid \mathbf X=\mathbf x) =
\frac{\exp(\beta_0+\mathbf x^T\boldsymbol\beta)}
{1+\exp(\beta_0+\mathbf x^T\boldsymbol\beta)}.
$$

The unregularized maximum likelihood estimator maximizes the log-likelihood. If the two classes can be **completely separated**, increasing the magnitude of a separating coefficient vector drives the fitted probabilities toward 0 and 1, without attaining a finite maximum likelihood estimate.

Below we create a toy **separable** dataset and show that unregularized fitting can produce huge coefficients or warnings, while regularization yields a stable, finite solution. 

### Simulate separable data

```{r separation-data}
set.seed(0)

x0 <- rnorm(10, mean = 0, sd = 1)
x1 <- rnorm(10, mean = 5, sd = 1)

separation_data <- data.frame(
  x = c(x0, x1),
  z = rnorm(20),
  y = c(rep(0, 10), rep(1, 10))
)

# Check whether the two observed groups are separated
max(x0) < min(x1)

head(separation_data)
```

### Fit ordinary logistic regression

```{r separation-glm}
# Warnings about fitted probabilities of 0 or 1 may appear.
fit_sep <- glm(y ~ x + z, data = separation_data, family = binomial())
summary(fit_sep)
coef(fit_sep)
```

```{r separation-plot, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.5}
x_grid <- data.frame(
  x = seq(min(separation_data$x) - 1,
          max(separation_data$x) + 1,
          length.out = 400),
  z = 0
)

x_grid$p <- predict(fit_sep, newdata = x_grid, type = "response")

ggplot(separation_data, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = factor(y)), size = 2.5) +
  geom_line(data = x_grid, aes(y = p), color = "darkgreen", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("0" = "steelblue", "1" = "firebrick"),
                     name = "Class") +
  labs(title = "Logistic regression with separated classes",
       x = "x", y = "Observed class / fitted probability") +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Fit ridge-regularized logistic regression

`glmnet()` minimizes a penalized loss. With `alpha = 0`, it uses an L2 (ridge) penalty. We specify a fixed positive `lambda` for illustration rather than choosing it by cross-validation.

```{r separation-ridge}
X_sep <- as.matrix(separation_data[, c("x", "z")])
y_sep <- separation_data$y

ridge_sep <- glmnet(X_sep, y_sep,
                    family = "binomial", alpha = 0, lambda = 0.1)
coef(ridge_sep)

x_new <- cbind(x = x_grid$x, z = 0)

x_grid$p_ridge <- as.numeric(
  predict(ridge_sep, newx = x_new,
          type = "response", s = 0.1)
)
```

```{r ridge-plot, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.5}
ggplot(separation_data, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = factor(y)), size = 2.5) +
  geom_line(data = x_grid, aes(y = p_ridge),
            color = "purple4", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("0" = "steelblue", "1" = "firebrick"),
                     name = "Class") +
  labs(title = "Ridge-regularized logistic regression",
       x = "x", y = "Observed class / fitted probability") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Key point:** Under complete separation, an unregularized logistic regression fit may not have finite MLEs; regularization yields finite coefficients for a positive penalty.

## 2. A reusable function for decision regions

The function below fits no model itself. Given a **fitted classifier** and two predictors, it creates a grid, predicts the class at each grid point, and colors the resulting decision regions. We will use it for both datasets.

```{r plot-helper}
plot_decision_regions <- function(model, data, features, response, title,
                                  grid_length = 180) {
  stopifnot(length(features) == 2)

  x_name <- features[1]
  y_name <- features[2]

  x_range <- range(data[[x_name]]) + c(-1, 1)
  y_range <- range(data[[y_name]]) + c(-1, 1)

  grid <- expand.grid(
    seq(x_range[1], x_range[2], length.out = grid_length),
    seq(y_range[1], y_range[2], length.out = grid_length)
  )
  names(grid) <- features

  # predict() returns class labels for glmnet-independent classifiers
  grid$predicted_class <- factor(predict(model, newdata = grid, type = "class"))
  plot_data <- data
  plot_data$observed_class <- factor(data[[response]])

  ggplot() +
    geom_raster(data = grid,
                aes(x = .data[[x_name]], y = .data[[y_name]],
                    fill = predicted_class), alpha = 0.3) +
    geom_point(data = plot_data,
               aes(x = .data[[x_name]], y = .data[[y_name]],
                   color = observed_class), size = 1.6, alpha = 0.8) +
    labs(title = title, x = x_name, y = y_name,
         fill = "Predicted", color = "Observed") +
    coord_cartesian(expand = FALSE) +
    theme_minimal()
}
```

**Note:** The helper is intended for the `glm`-independent `MASS::lda`, `MASS::qda` and `nnet::multinom` classifiers below, plus the logistic regression wrapper defined in the Smarket section. Its use of `type = "class"` will not work directly with a base R `glm` object.

## 3. Binary classification: Smarket

The `Smarket` dataset has 1,250 observations of daily S&P 500 returns from 2001 to 2005. `Lag1` through `Lag5` are percentage returns on the previous five trading days, `Volume` is trading volume, and `Direction` indicates whether the market moved **Up** or **Down**.

```{r smarket-explore}
data(Smarket)
head(Smarket)
str(Smarket)
cor(Smarket[, sapply(Smarket, is.numeric)])
```

```{r smarket-volume, fig.width=7, fig.height=4}
ggplot(Smarket, aes(x = seq_along(Volume), y = Volume)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Smarket: Trading volume over time",
       x = "Trading day (index)", y = "Volume") +
  theme_minimal()
```

### 3.1 Logistic regression using all lag variables and Volume

Binary logistic regression models the posterior probability **directly**:

$$
\log\left(\frac{P(Y=\mathrm{Up}\mid\mathbf x)}
{1-P(Y=\mathrm{Up}\mid\mathbf x)}\right)
=\beta_0+\mathbf x^T\boldsymbol\beta.
$$

With a 0.5 probability cutoff, its decision boundary is linear in the original predictors.

```{r sigmoid, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
t <- seq(-8, 8, length.out = 400)
plot(t, plogis(t), type = "l", lwd = 2,
     main = "Sigmoid function", xlab = "t", ylab = "P(Y = 1)")
```

```{r smarket-allvars}
logit_all <- glm(Direction ~ Lag1 + Lag2 + Lag3 + Lag4 + Lag5 + Volume,
                 data = Smarket, family = binomial())
summary(logit_all)

prob_all <- predict(logit_all, type = "response")
head(prob_all, 10)

pred_all <- factor(ifelse(prob_all > 0.5, "Up", "Down"),
                   levels = levels(Smarket$Direction))

# Rows: predictions; columns: true classes
table(Predicted = pred_all, Truth = Smarket$Direction)
mean(pred_all == Smarket$Direction)  # Training accuracy
```

### 3.2 Evaluate on a held-out year

Train on observations from **2001–2004** and test on **2005**. This chronological split avoids training on observations that occur after the test observations.

```{r smarket-split}
train <- subset(Smarket, Year < 2005)
test  <- subset(Smarket, Year == 2005)

nrow(train)
nrow(test)

logit_all_train <- glm(Direction ~ Lag1 + Lag2 + Lag3 + Lag4 + Lag5 + Volume,
                       data = train, family = binomial())

prob_test <- predict(logit_all_train, newdata = test, type = "response")
pred_test <- factor(ifelse(prob_test > 0.5, "Up", "Down"),
                    levels = levels(Smarket$Direction))

table(Predicted = pred_test, Truth = test$Direction)
mean(pred_test == test$Direction)  # Test accuracy
```

```{r smarket-baseline}
# Accuracy from predicting the most frequent class in the training set
majority_class <- names(which.max(table(train$Direction)))
majority_class
mean(test$Direction == majority_class)
```

### 3.3 Refit using only Lag1 and Lag2

Using just two predictors lets us visualize the decision boundaries. For a fair comparison, all three models use **exactly the same training and test data**.

```{r smarket-two-features}
features <- c("Lag1", "Lag2")

# Fit an ordinary (unpenalized) logistic regression, equivalent to glm(..., binomial).
logit_two <- glm(Direction ~ Lag1 + Lag2,
                 data = train, family = binomial())

# Wrapper providing class predictions for the plotting helper
logit_class <- list(fit = logit_two)
class(logit_class) <- "logit_class"

predict.logit_class <- function(object, newdata, type = "class", ...) {
  p <- predict(object$fit, newdata = newdata, type = "response")
  factor(ifelse(p > 0.5, "Up", "Down"), levels = c("Down", "Up"))
}

plot_decision_regions(logit_class, train, features, "Direction",
                      "Logistic regression: Smarket training decision regions")

pred_logit <- predict(logit_class, newdata = test)
table(Predicted = pred_logit, Truth = test$Direction)
mean(pred_logit == test$Direction)
```


### 3.4 Linear discriminant analysis (LDA)

LDA assumes the predictor distributions within the classes are multivariate Gaussian with a **shared covariance matrix**:

$$
\mathbf X\mid Y=k \sim N_p(\boldsymbol\mu_k,\boldsymbol\Sigma).
$$

Its discriminant score is

$$
\delta_k(\mathbf x)
=\mathbf x^T\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}\boldsymbol\mu_k
-\frac12\boldsymbol\mu_k^T\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}\boldsymbol\mu_k
+\log\pi_k.
$$

```{r smarket-lda}
lda_fit <- lda(Direction ~ Lag1 + Lag2, data = train)
lda_fit

# MASS::predict() returns a list; $class contains class labels.
pred_lda <- predict(lda_fit, newdata = test)$class

table(Predicted = pred_lda, Truth = test$Direction)
mean(pred_lda == test$Direction)
```

For plotting, wrap LDA's output in a classifier that returns labels:

```{r smarket-lda-plot, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
lda_class <- list(fit = lda_fit)
class(lda_class) <- "lda_class"

predict.lda_class <- function(object, newdata, type = "class", ...) {
  predict(object$fit, newdata = newdata)$class
}

plot_decision_regions(lda_class, train, features, "Direction",
                      "LDA: Smarket training decision regions")
```

### 3.5 Quadratic discriminant analysis (QDA)

QDA assumes class-conditional Gaussians but allows the covariance matrix to **differ by class**:

$$
\mathbf X\mid Y=k \sim N_p(\boldsymbol\mu_k,\boldsymbol\Sigma_k).
$$

The discriminant score contains a class-specific quadratic term:

$$
\delta_k(\mathbf x)
=-\frac12\log |\boldsymbol\Sigma_k|
-\frac12(\mathbf x-\boldsymbol\mu_k)^T
\boldsymbol\Sigma_k^{-1}(\mathbf x-\boldsymbol\mu_k)
+\log\pi_k.
$$

```{r smarket-qda}
qda_fit <- qda(Direction ~ Lag1 + Lag2, data = train)
qda_fit

pred_qda <- predict(qda_fit, newdata = test)$class

table(Predicted = pred_qda, Truth = test$Direction)
mean(pred_qda == test$Direction)
```

```{r smarket-qda-plot, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
qda_class <- list(fit = qda_fit)
class(qda_class) <- "qda_class"

predict.qda_class <- function(object, newdata, type = "class", ...) {
  predict(object$fit, newdata = newdata)$class
}

plot_decision_regions(qda_class, train, features, "Direction",
                      "QDA: Smarket training decision regions")
```

### 3.6 Compare Smarket test accuracy

```{r smarket-comparison}
results_smarket <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Logistic regression", "LDA", "QDA"),
  Test_Accuracy = c(
    mean(pred_logit == test$Direction),
    mean(pred_lda == test$Direction),
    mean(pred_qda == test$Direction)
  )
)
results_smarket[order(-results_smarket$Test_Accuracy), ]
```

## 4. Multiclass classification: Iris

The built-in `iris` dataset contains **three species**, with **50 observations per species**. To visualize decision regions in two dimensions, we use **petal length** and **petal width** only.

```{r iris-data}
data(iris)
head(iris)
table(iris$Species)

iris_two <- iris[, c("Petal.Length", "Petal.Width", "Species")]

# All three models are fit and displayed on the full iris dataset to
# reproduce the original tutorial's illustrative decision-region plots.
# These are NOT held-out test evaluations.
```

### 4.1 Multinomial logistic regression (softmax)

For $K$ classes, multinomial logistic regression models the class probabilities directly:

$$
P(Y=k\mid\mathbf x)
=\frac{\exp(\beta_{k0}+\mathbf x^T\boldsymbol\beta_k)}
{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(\beta_{j0}+\mathbf x^T\boldsymbol\beta_j)}.
$$

One class can be used as the reference class for identifiability. The **pairwise decision boundaries** are linear in the original predictors.

```{r iris-multinom, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
multinom_fit <- multinom(Species ~ Petal.Length + Petal.Width,
                        data = iris_two, trace = FALSE)
summary(multinom_fit)

plot_decision_regions(multinom_fit, iris_two,
                      c("Petal.Length", "Petal.Width"), "Species",
                      "Multinomial logistic regression: Iris")
```


### 4.2 Multiclass LDA

```{r iris-lda, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
iris_lda <- lda(Species ~ Petal.Length + Petal.Width, data = iris_two)
iris_lda_class <- list(fit = iris_lda)
class(iris_lda_class) <- "lda_class"

plot_decision_regions(iris_lda_class, iris_two,
                      c("Petal.Length", "Petal.Width"), "Species",
                      "LDA: Iris")
```

### 4.3 Multiclass QDA

```{r iris-qda, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
iris_qda <- qda(Species ~ Petal.Length + Petal.Width, data = iris_two)
iris_qda_class <- list(fit = iris_qda)
class(iris_qda_class) <- "qda_class"

plot_decision_regions(iris_qda_class, iris_two,
                      c("Petal.Length", "Petal.Width"), "Species",
                      "QDA: Iris")
```


## 5. Wrap-up: What should you remember?

| Method | What is modelled? | Covariance assumption | Decision boundary in original features |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Binary / multinomial logistic regression | $P(Y=k\mid \mathbf X)$ directly | No Gaussian covariance assumption | Linear pairwise boundaries |
| LDA | Gaussian $\mathbf X\mid Y=k$ | Same covariance across classes | Linear pairwise boundaries |
| QDA | Gaussian $\mathbf X\mid Y=k$ | Different covariance by class | Quadratic pairwise boundaries |

**Final comprehension check (TA-led, 3 minutes)**

1. A classification problem has approximately Gaussian predictors within each class, but the classes have very different covariance matrices. Which method would you consider first, and why?
2. A training dataset has only a few observations per class and many predictors. Which may be more stable: LDA or QDA? Why?
3. A logistic regression fit reports very large coefficients and warnings about perfect prediction. What issue should you investigate? Name one potential remedy.
4. A model achieves 95% training accuracy and 60% test accuracy. Which value is most relevant to estimating performance on unseen data, and what might explain the difference?

**Reminder:** A flexible decision boundary does not guarantee better test performance. Evaluate candidate classifiers on held-out data, and consider whether their assumptions are appropriate.
